mcqs.question: Which of the following comparisons best explains why handloom production survived despite the rise of mechanised factories?

options.A: Handloom products were cheaper than machine‑made goods, attracting mass markets.
options.B: Handloom weavers could quickly switch to producing steel goods, diversifying their income.
options.C: Handloom fabrics offered unique designs and cultural value that machines could not replicate.
options.D: Handloom workers received higher wages than factory workers, making the sector more profitable.

mcqs.answer: Handloom fabrics offered unique designs and cultural value that machines could not replicate.
mcqs.explanation: Handloom production survived mainly because its products carried traditional designs, regional motifs and cultural significance that machine‑made textiles lacked. This uniqueness created a niche market that valued authenticity over low cost. Options A, B and D are incorrect: handloom goods were generally more expensive, weavers did not shift to steel production, and wages were lower than in factories.

mcqs.question: In the context of traditional handloom clusters, which statement correctly describes specialisation and product differentiation?

options.A: All weavers in a cluster produce identical plain cotton cloths to achieve economies of scale.
options.B: Each weaver focuses on a particular type of fabric or design, creating varied products for different market segments.
options.C: Specialisation means abandoning traditional motifs and adopting only modern synthetic fabrics.
options.D: Product differentiation is achieved by reducing the quality of yarn to lower production costs.

mcqs.answer: Each weaver focuses on a particular type of fabric or design, creating varied products for different market segments.
mcqs.explanation: Traditional handloom clusters often exhibit specialisation where individual weavers master specific fabrics (e.g., silk, khadi) or designs (e.g., Banarasi, Kasavu). This creates product differentiation, allowing them to cater to varied consumer preferences. Option A ignores differentiation, C misrepresents specialisation, and D confuses differentiation with quality reduction.

mcqs.question: One major effect of the influx of machine‑made textile imports on Indian handloom weavers was:

options.A: A sudden increase in the wages of handloom workers.
options.B: A decline in demand for hand‑woven fabrics, leading to loss of livelihood for many weavers.
options.C: The immediate closure of all handloom units across the country.
options.D: An increase in the export of handloom products to Europe.

mcqs.answer: A decline in demand for hand‑woven fabrics, leading to loss of livelihood for many weavers.
mcqs.explanation: Machine‑made imports were cheaper and produced in large quantities, which reduced the market for hand‑woven fabrics. This caused many weavers to lose income and, in some cases, abandon the trade. Options A, C, and D are inaccurate: wages fell, not rose; many handloom units survived albeit under stress; exports did not surge because of competition.

mcqs.learning_point: Identify strategies used by traditional producers
mcqs.question: Which of the following strategies was commonly adopted by traditional handloom producers to cope with competition from machine‑made textiles?

options.A: Switching entirely to the production of plastic goods.
options.B: Forming cooperatives to collectively market their unique designs.
options.C: Increasing the price of their products to match factory rates.
options.D: Reducing the quality of yarn to cut production costs.

mcqs.answer: Forming cooperatives to collectively market their unique designs.
mcqs.explanation: Cooperatives allowed weavers to pool resources, standardise quality, and promote distinctive regional designs, helping them compete with mass‑produced goods. Options A and D describe abandoning traditional craft, while C would make handloom products less competitive.

mcqs.question: How does handloom production differ from powerloom production?

options.A: Handloom production uses manual power and retains traditional designs, whereas powerloom relies on electricity and produces uniform, mass‑produced fabrics.
options.B: Handloom production is faster than powerloom production and always cheaper.
options.C: Powerloom production requires skilled artisans for each piece, while handloom can be fully automated.
options.D: Both handloom and powerloom produce identical fabrics, differing only in the type of yarn used.

mcqs.answer: Handloom production uses manual power and retains traditional designs, whereas powerloom relies on electricity and produces uniform, mass‑produced fabrics.
mcqs.explanation: Handloom weaving is done manually, preserving regional motifs and allowing customization, while powerloom uses mechanised looms powered by electricity, leading to standardized, high‑volume output. Options B, C, and D misstate speed, skill requirements, and product similarity.

mcqs.question: A village of handloom weavers decides that each family will specialize in a distinct type of fabric—one in silk, another in cotton, another in wool, and another in patterned khadi. What economic advantage does this specialisation provide?

options.A: It allows the village to produce a single, uniform product that competes on price alone.
options.B: It creates a range of differentiated products, attracting diverse customers and reducing direct competition among the weavers.
options.C: It forces all weavers to use the same raw material, lowering procurement costs.
options.D: It eliminates the need for any marketing because each product sells itself.

mcqs.answer: It creates a range of differentiated products, attracting diverse customers and reducing direct competition among the weavers.
mcqs.explanation: By specializing in different fabrics and designs, the weavers offer varied products, catering to multiple market niches and avoiding price wars. This is product differentiation. Option A ignores differentiation, C is false about raw material, and D overstates the effect of specialization.

mcqs.question: When cheap, machine‑made cotton shirts from Britain entered Indian markets in the 19th century, many handloom weavers in Gujarat experienced:

options.A: A surge in orders for their hand‑woven shirts because consumers preferred local products.
options.B: A reduction in sales leading some weavers to shift to weaving finer silk fabrics for niche markets.
options.C: An immediate increase in government subsidies that fully compensated their losses.
options.D: A transition to producing metal tools as a direct replacement for textiles.

mcqs.answer: A reduction in sales leading some weavers to shift to weaving finer silk fabrics for niche markets.
mcqs.explanation: The influx of inexpensive British cotton shirts reduced demand for locally made cotton handloom shirts, prompting some weavers to adapt by targeting niche segments such as silk or high‑quality fabrics. Options A, C, and D are historically inaccurate.

mcqs.learning_point: Identify strategies used by traditional producers
mcqs.question: Ramesh, a handloom weaver, notices that his sales are falling due to imported synthetic fabrics. He decides to (i) obtain a Geographical Indication (GI) tag for his regional design, (ii) collaborate with a local boutique to showcase his work, and (iii) increase the price of his cloths by 50%. Which of these actions is most likely to be an effective long‑term strategy?

options.A: Only (i) – the GI tag alone will protect his market.
options.B: Only (ii) – partnering with a boutique will guarantee higher sales.
options.C: Only (iii) – raising prices will make his products appear premium.
options.D: Both (i) and (ii) – the GI tag adds authenticity while the boutique partnership expands market reach.

mcqs.answer: Both (i) and (ii) – the GI tag adds authenticity while the boutique partnership expands market reach.
mcqs.explanation: A GI tag legally recognises the uniqueness of a regional product, enhancing its market value, while collaboration with a boutique provides a sales channel and visibility. Raising prices alone (iii) may deter buyers, and a GI tag without market access (i alone) is insufficient. Hence, combining (i) and (ii) offers a sustainable advantage.
